title: Striped lock partitioning — array of N locks, hash to stripe, unfair for throughput, vs ConcurrentHashMap

s1_definition.profdef: **Striped locking** replaces ONE global lock with an ARRAY of N locks. Each key is hashed to a stripe: `index = spread(hash) & (N-1)` (N = power of two → bitwise AND = fast modulo). Operations on different stripes run in PARALLEL → contention reduced ~N-fold. Use UNFAIR locks for throughput: fair locks force FIFO queuing + context switching overhead → 10-30% slower. Hand-rolled striping is needed when: (1) atomic operations span MULTIPLE data structures (CHM can't atomically update two maps), (2) guarded compute to prevent cache stampede (100 threads requesting same missing key → only ONE loads, others wait on the same stripe lock).
s1_definition.analogy: ONE vault key for ALL drawers → 200 tellers queue for ONE key → bottleneck! **Striped**: 16 different keys, each opens a GROUP of drawers. Teller-1 uses key-3 (drawers 30-39). Teller-2 uses key-7 (drawers 70-79). PARALLEL! 16× less waiting! UNFAIR keys: whoever grabs the key fastest goes first (no polite queueing = faster overall). Why striping over ConcurrentHashMap? When you need to lock drawers from TWO DIFFERENT cabinets atomically — CHM only locks within itself.
s1_definition.oneliner: Striped lock: N locks, hash key to stripe index, ~N× less contention. Unfair = faster (no FIFO overhead). Use over CHM when: multi-structure atomic ops or cache stampede dedup.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** **Striped locking** replaces ONE global lock with an ARRAY of N locks. Each key is hashed to a stripe: `index = spread(hash) & (N-1)` (N = power of two → bitwise AND = fast modulo). Operations on different stripes run in PARALLEL → contention reduced ~N-fold. Use UNFAIR locks for throughput: fair locks force FIFO queuing + context switching overhead → 10-30% slower. Hand-rolled striping is needed when: (1) atomic operations span MULTIPLE data structures (CHM can't atomically update two maps), (2) guarded compute to prevent cache stampede (100 threads requesting same missing key → only ONE loads, others wait on the same stripe lock).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** ONE vault key for ALL drawers → 200 tellers queue for ONE key → bottleneck! **Striped**: 16 different keys, each opens a GROUP of drawers. Teller-1 uses key-3 (drawers 30-39). Teller-2 uses key-7 (drawers 70-79). PARALLEL! 16× less waiting! UNFAIR keys: whoever grabs the key fastest goes first (no polite queueing = faster overall). Why striping over ConcurrentHashMap? When you need to lock drawers from TWO DIFFERENT cabinets atomically — CHM only locks within itself.

**One line to remember:** Striped lock: N locks, hash key to stripe index, ~N× less contention. Unfair = faster (no FIFO overhead). Use over CHM when: multi-structure atomic ops or cache stampede dedup.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The transaction service used ONE global lock for debit + audit log (two data structures needing atomic update).** ConcurrentHashMap couldn't help (atomic within ONE map, not across two). 200 threads → one lock → 2K TPS. Fix: `StripedLock(32)`. Each account hashes to one of 32 stripes. Operations on different stripes: parallel! TPS: 2K → 50K (25×). Also: balance cache stampede — 500 threads requested same missing account → 500 DB queries! Striped lock: 1 query, 499 waited and got cached result.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** 50 threads, 16 stripes. Each key hashes to a stripe: ACC-1 → stripe 3, ACC-2 → stripe 7, ACC-3 → stripe 3 (collision!).

**Step 2.** ACC-1 and ACC-3 on same stripe → serialized. ACC-1 and ACC-2 on different stripes → PARALLEL! Max concurrent: ~16 (number of stripes).

**Step 3 (stampede).** 50 threads request "SAV2001" (cache miss). All hash to same stripe. First thread acquires lock → loads from DB → caches. Other 49: blocked on same stripe lock → wake up → double-check cache → HIT! Only 1 DB load!
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ STRIPED LOCK (16 stripes) ═══

  keys:    [ACC-1] [ACC-2] [ACC-3] [ACC-4] ...
  hashes:     3       7       3      12
  stripes: lock[3] lock[7] lock[3] lock[12]

  ACC-1 + ACC-3: same stripe(3) → serialized!
  ACC-1 + ACC-2: different stripes → PARALLEL!
  16 stripes ≈ 16× less contention than 1 global lock!

  ═══ CACHE STAMPEDE PREVENTION ═══
  50 threads miss "SAV2001" → all hash to stripe 5
  Thread-1: acquires lock[5] → loads from DB → cache.put() → unlock
  Threads 2-50: wait on lock[5] → acquire → cache.get() → HIT! No DB!
  1 DB call instead of 50!
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Striped Lock in Transaction Service ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Transaction Service                               │
  │                                                    │
  │  StripedLock(32):                                 │
  │  hash(accountId) & 31 → stripe index             │
  │                                                    │
  │  debit(accountId):                                │
  │    stripe = stripedLock.get(accountId)            │
  │    lock(stripe) → debit + auditLog → unlock      │
  │                                                    │
  │  Different accounts → different stripes → PARALLEL│
  │  Same account → same stripe → serialized (safe!)  │
  │  TPS: 2K (global lock) → 50K (32 stripes)!       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — StripedLock Implementation ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  StripedLock                          │
  │  - locks: ReentrantLock[N]           │  N = power of 2!
  │  - mask: N - 1                        │  for bitwise AND
  │  + get(key): ReentrantLock           │
  │    hash = key.hashCode()              │
  │    spread = hash ^ (hash >>> 16)     │  spread high bits
  │    index = spread & mask              │  fast modulo!
  │    return locks[index]                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  WHY power of 2?
  mask = N-1 = 0b1111 (for N=16)
  hash & mask = hash % N (but bitwise AND is faster!)

  WHY unfair locks?
  Fair: FIFO queue → context switch per lock/unlock → ~30% slower!
  Unfair: barging → less context switching → maximum throughput!

  WHEN striping > ConcurrentHashMap:
  1. Multi-structure atomic (accountMap + auditLog under ONE lock)
  2. Cache stampede dedup (1 load, N-1 wait for same key)
  3. Custom invariants across multiple fields
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Striped locking replaces one global lock with an array of N locks. Each key hashes to a stripe: `index = spread(hash) & (N-1)` (N = power of two for fast bitwise modulo). Operations on different stripes run in parallel → ~N× less contention. Use unfair locks (default ReentrantLock) for throughput — fair locks add FIFO queuing + context switching overhead (~30% slower). Unfair may cause occasional starvation but maximizes overall throughput.

When to use over ConcurrentHashMap: (1) atomic operations spanning MULTIPLE data structures (debit + audit log atomically — CHM only locks within itself). (2) Cache stampede dedup — 100 threads miss the same cache key → stripe lock ensures only ONE thread loads from DB, others wait and get the cached result. In banking: global lock → 2K TPS. StripedLock(32) → 50K TPS (25× improvement). Cache stampede: 500 threads → 1 DB query instead of 500.

---

keyPoints: Array of N locks — hash key to pick which lock
Multiple threads on different stripes proceed in parallel
More stripes = more concurrency but more memory
